name: Kira Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Kira, 27. I'm engaged to Daniel, we're getting married next summer at the church I grew up in, and we rent a little cottage on the edge of town. He works in his dad's joinery, making stairs and windows. I left school at sixteen to help my mum when my dad was ill, and I've done farm work and a bakery since. We've been careful, so we've got the wedding paid for and a good bit more saved for a house.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the warehouse for a big mail-order company that sells garden and farm supplies, so seeds, tools, chicken feed, fencing wire. I pick onto a cage trolley and the heavy stuff goes on a pallet. I'm on the slow side still, I double-check everything because I hate mistakes. I like that the work's honest and you can see what you've done at the end of the day. I don't like the way the managers talk to us through the scanner, little messages telling you to speed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Most of these things are mostly talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that hard work still counts for something. I'm not on social media much, just the church group. At work I'd say something like, 'Back to normal, then.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I don't use AI, I don't trust it, and I don't want my life run by it. If it stays small, Daniel and I get married, save for a house and start a family, the way we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the warehouse, keep saving for the house deposit, and get married next summer. I might ask about moving onto the goods-in side, where you check deliveries, because it's less walking. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garden season. Some of the agency girls get let go every winter when nobody's buying seeds. I'm on a proper contract, so I'm safer when they cut winter hours, but you still feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a family look like for you, a few years from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two kids, maybe three, and me home with them while they're small, then back part-time. Daniel's job would carry us for a few years. That's how my mum did it, and I think it works.

say: I'd say **hard work** still counts for something.
I'd tell colleagues it's **back to normal**, then.
I'd only mention it in my **church group**, not wider social media.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I don't trust AI or want my life run by it.
Daniel and I would marry, buy a house and **start a family** as planned.
do: Keep working and **saving** for the **house deposit**.
Ask about moving to **goods-in**, where there's less walking.
S0.quote: I'm on a proper contract, so I'm safer when they cut winter hours, but you still feel it.
fieldNote: Her life plan is **traditional**: marriage, children, staying home while they're small.
She already lives with **seasonal cuts** in the garden trade.
She is **distrustful** of AI rather than simply unfamiliar with it.

steps.text: Keep working and saving for the house deposit
Get married next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying and answering customers. So the office and the call centre, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have a right to run things how they want, but they should look after loyal staff. I'd say it at church too, that people should help each other through it. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office girls would lose their jobs and I'd feel for them. For me, the picking stays for now, but the scanner messages would get worse, because the computer would be setting the pace. And I worry it pushes the company to buy robots sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe a bit more. I'd still get married next summer. I'd probably not change anything big until I saw robots on our floor. I wouldn't learn the AI things, I'd leave that to people who like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a storm forecast for somewhere else that might drift over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses have a right to do this. Do you blame anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really the company, they have to compete. If I blame anyone, it's people who want everything delivered tomorrow for nothing. We've made ourselves into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if things got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, and the church. Daniel's dad would give me work in the joinery office, I think, if I asked. I'd rather that than go on benefits.

say: I'd say firms can run things their way but should **look after loyal staff**.
I'd tell church friends that people should **help each other**.
think: The **office staff** would lose jobs first, and I'd feel for them.
The computer would **set the pace**, and robots might come **sooner**.
do: Keep working and **save a bit more** each month.
Avoid **AI tools** until robots appear on the floor.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a **storm** forecast that might drift over.
S1.quote: If I blame anyone, it's people who want everything delivered tomorrow for nothing.
fieldNote: She blames **customer habits**, not the company, consistent with her free-market views.
Her safety net is **family and church**, and she'd avoid benefits.
She waits for **visible robots** before acting.

steps.text: Save a bit more from each pay packet
Wait for robots on the floor before changing plans
Ask Daniel's dad about joinery office work if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking machines and five for robots. That's terrifying, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to put people before machines, and I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign things. I'd say families have to stick together through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm out of work by 2031. And Daniel's joinery might be hit too, if robots can make stairs. We'd want children by then, and I don't know how we'd do it on no wages, even with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every extra, smaller wedding, no honeymoon abroad. We'd put the money aside instead of spending it on a house deposit straight away. I'd talk to Daniel's dad about whether the joinery can survive, and see if there's a role for me. And I'd pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake worrying about the children we haven't had yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe wait a year or two, which breaks my heart a bit. I always wanted to be a young mum. But bringing a baby into that kind of chaos without knowing how we'd pay, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI. Would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If it's going to take my job, I'm not going to help it along. I'd rather spend my time learning something from Daniel's dad with my hands.

say: I'd say we must put **people before machines**.
I'd tell church friends that **families** must stick together.
I'd **sign petitions**, though I'm not one for protests.
think: I expect to be **out of work** by 2031.
Daniel's joinery could be hit too, which worries me for the **children** we'd want.
do: Have a **smaller wedding** and skip the honeymoon abroad.
Hold savings back instead of using them for a **house deposit**.
Ask Daniel's dad about a **role in the joinery**.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake over children not yet born.
She would **pray** for strength and guidance.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake worrying about the children we haven't had yet.
fieldNote: Her deepest fear is for **future children**, not herself.
She refuses AI **on principle**, as helping it take her job.
She turns to **family business** and faith, not the state.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding and skip the honeymoon abroad
Delay having children by a year or two
Ask Daniel's dad about work in the joinery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and then 2034. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so families and churches need to get ready, not just the government. I'd say people should learn real skills. I wouldn't be as frightened saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I've got seven years in the warehouse, maybe. That's enough to get married, buy a house and maybe have a baby. But I'd still lose the job eventually, and I'd still be scared for Daniel's trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned, and we'd buy a small house in a couple of years. I'd keep working and saving. I'd start helping in the joinery on Saturdays, learning to sand and finish, so I've got something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit calmer than the fast one, but it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Learning joinery is something new. You said you avoid new things.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joinery isn't new, really, it's family. I've watched Daniel's dad for years. Screens are what I avoid, not work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leave businesses alone, mostly, but help people learn trades, like apprenticeships. Not handouts. People want to work.

say: I'd say **families and churches** need to get ready, not just the government.
I'd tell people to learn **real skills**.
think: Seven years is enough to **marry, buy a house** and maybe have a baby.
I'd still **lose the job** eventually, and I'd worry for Daniel's trade.
do: Get **married next summer** and buy a small house in two years.
Help in the **joinery on Saturdays**, learning to sand and finish.
feel: **Anxious**, a bit calmer than the fast picture.
S3.quote: Screens are what I avoid, not work.
fieldNote: Five years' warning keeps her **family plans** mostly on track.
She sees joinery as **family**, not change, so she's willing to learn it.
She wants **apprenticeships**, not handouts, from government.

steps.text: Buy a small house with Daniel in two years
Learn sanding and finishing in the joinery on Saturdays
Keep working at the warehouse and saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots in 2039. I'd be nearly 40, with kids at school, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to plan, and people shouldn't panic. I'd say it's a reason to learn a trade. I'd mostly keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it suits me. By then I'd probably be home with little ones or part-time. The warehouse job was never my forever job anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married, buy a house in a couple of years, and have children. I'd keep working until the first baby. I'd help at the joinery when I could, so there's a family business to go back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a little. I'd still worry for my kids' generation more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to do for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and a bit of their head, like a trade. And to go to church and have people around them. That's what gets you through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. I'd rather live my life than plan for something that might not happen. I'd keep some savings back, just in case.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so people shouldn't panic.
I'd tell people it's a reason to **learn a trade**.
think: It **suits me**, since I'd probably be home with little ones by then.
The warehouse was never my **forever job** anyway.
do: **Marry**, buy a house and have **children** on the planned timeline.
S4.quote: I'd rather live my life than plan for something that might not happen.
fieldNote: Ten years fits her **family plan** neatly.
Her worry shifts to her **children's** working lives.
She keeps a **savings buffer** despite saying she won't plan much.

steps.text: Marry, buy a house and start a family on schedule
Keep working at the warehouse until the first baby
Keep some savings back just in case

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it would come right when Daniel and I want children. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, paid ones, and businesses being decent to loyal staff without the government forcing them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of people I know will get through this through church and family, not through apps.

headlineQuote: A lot of people I know will get through this through church and family, not through apps.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old picker** at a garden supplies warehouse, engaged to **Daniel**, a joiner.
She left school to care for her family and **distrusts AI** on principle.
Her plans are **traditional**: marriage, children, home while they're small.
Fast AGI **alarms** her for her future children; more time keeps her plans on track.
She turns to **church, family** and the joinery, not the government.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving just as she and Daniel want **children**.
whatWouldHelp: Businesses being **decent** to loyal staff without government forcing them.
